\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through multi-sample generation promises quality improvements for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but which confidence signals best serve quality estimation versus sample selection remains unclear.
Under constrained decoding---the standard inference regime for schema-compliant IE---we compare five signals from three families (structural, surface, model-internal) across NER (three datasets) and RE (SciERC, preliminary) with two 8B-parameter model families.
For quality estimation, the strongest signals achieve Spearman $\rho{=}0.38$ and AUROC${=}0.75$, with ranking and classification favoring different signals depending on task complexity.
However, this estimation does not translate into selection gains: four of five signals are instance-level by construction, and log-probability---the only per-sample signal---fails to outperform greedy decoding ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
We term this the \textit{correlation-selection gap} and diagnose its mechanism: log-probability scores are severely compressed under constrained decoding, but in the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated, log-probability becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
Signal rankings further depend on task difficulty, with consistent ordering across models but model-dependent magnitude.
These results reframe consistency signals as quality estimators rather than output selectors for structured IE under constrained decoding.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and logprob exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs are unparseable.
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is that, under constrained decoding, consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators but poor sample selectors for structured IE.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC NER and EM leads AUROC${=}0.75$, both practically useful for quality-aware routing.
Yet we find no statistically significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy decoding on best-of-$N$ selection ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
We term this the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} are hard, not \textit{which output} is best.
This gap is not obvious \textit{a priori}: minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding---selecting the sample maximizing expected utility against the candidate set---succeeds in machine translation \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding}.
Our consensus-proximity strategy (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) instantiates MBR with structural utility functions; that this approach fails for IE is a non-trivial finding that we trace to the instance-level nature of structural utility (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. Left: consistency signals (here VC) predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1 ($\rho{\approx}0.38$, AUROC${\approx}0.69$). Right: the same instance-level signal assigns identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input, precluding sample selection; consensus-proximity selection (choosing the sample closest to the consensus output) does not recover per-sample discrimination. No signal significantly outperforms greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A systematic multi-family comparison of confidence signals for generative IE under constrained decoding.}
    We evaluate five signals from three families on quality estimation for NER and RE.
    VC achieves the strongest $\rho{=}0.38$ while EM leads AUROC${=}0.75$; signal rankings depend on both task complexity and evaluation metric, with structural signals leading rank correlation on complex schemas (SciERC) and surface signals leading on simpler tasks (CoNLL)---an ordering directionally consistent across model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.

    \item \textbf{Identification and mechanistic diagnosis of the correlation-selection gap.}
    Within this standard deployment regime, we demonstrate that strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom).
    Four of five signals are instance-level by construction; log-probability---the only per-sample signal---also fails.
    Mechanistic diagnosis traces this largely to constrained-decoding-induced score compression (60\% of instances effectively tied), with the non-compressed subset confirming logprob is an effective selector when resolution is available ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
    MBR decoding with structural utility functions similarly fails, as utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks; when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$).
5	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
6	When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
7	
8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
9	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
10	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
11	\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
12	Under constrained decoding, logprob scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
13	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (logprob range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), logprob \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
14	This diagnostic confirms that logprob carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
15	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
16	
17	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
18	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
19	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
20	
21	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
22	The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
23	Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses logprob resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
24

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
Under constrained decoding, logprob scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (logprob range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), logprob \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that logprob carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses logprob resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

content.thinking:
Now I have the full experimental landscape. Let me compile my deep analysis.

Key observations from the registry:
1. Extensive experiments: 79 total, covering NER/RE on SciERC, CoNLL, WNUT-17 with Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B
2. Selection consistently fails: No experiment shows significant selection improvement over greedy
3. Oracle headroom is real: NER 13-18pp, RE 18-23pp
4. Score compression is documented: 60% tied at ε=0.05
5. Non-tied subset works: +2.9pp, p=0.01


6. The experiments are comprehensive within their scope, but they're all operating in the same constrained regime—8B models with unsupervised signals and fixed decoding constraints. The core issue is that most of the gap between greedy and oracle is actually definitional: four of the five signals failing is almost tautological, leaving only the logprob failure and score compression as genuinely empirical findings. Without a clear "so what" moment or a path forward, the paper reads more like a diagnostic than a contribution.

The non-tied subset result is the real lever here—showing that logprob does contain per-sample quality information when the range is sufficient. That's the insight that could reframe the whole work from "here's what doesn't work" to "here's where the signal actually lives."

The critical next step is testing whether this gap is specific to constrained decoding or more fundamental. Running the same analysis on free-form decoding would either confirm the mechanism (higher variance, better selection) or reveal the problem is universal rather than regime-specific. Either outcome strengthens the paper—one by pinpointing the bottleneck, the other by showing the finding matters broadly.

For the free-form ablation, I'd need to regenerate samples without Outlines constraints and accept whatever parse failures occur, then compare logprob distributions and selection metrics on the parseable outputs. The cost is manageable—maybe 2-4 hours on a single GPU given the parse rates should stay decent with fine-tuned models.

Beyond that, a supervised verifier could add real impact: a small classifier trained on existing samples to predict whether an output is among the best or exceeds a quality threshold, using something like DeBERTa as the encoder.  It's more involved—probably 1-2 days of work—but it would establish an upper bound on what unsupervised signals can achieve and show whether the gap is actually closable, which makes a negative result more constructive.

For temperature sensitivity, I could sweep across T=0.3 to 1.0 to see if compression holds steady or drops at lower temperatures. Early results suggest it's stable, but a wider range would strengthen that claim.

The hybrid approach seems most promising if feasible—combining constrained decoding with learned ranking or filtering to push performance further. constrained decoding for structure but free-form logprob for selection:
1. Generate N samples with constrained decoding (for valid outputs)
2. ALSO generate one sample free-form (for logprob reference)
3. Use free-form logprob to score the constrained samples

Or: generate free-form, filter parseable, select among parseable using logprob.

This would be a PRACTICAL SOLUTION, not just a diagnosis.

**My recommendation priority:**

[severity: critical] 6 轮 3.0/5 根本原因分析 + 突破路径

## 1. 为什么 6 轮纹丝不动

**根本原因不是 framing，是 substance。**

6 轮迭代一直在优化同一组发现的呈现方式——每轮修改的都是"怎么说"，没有改过"说什么"。但评分瓶颈不在修辞，在于论文的贡献结构有一个 built-in ceiling：

**贡献结构的三重弱点：**

(A) **核心发现 80% 是同义反复。** 4/5 信号是 instance-level aggregate → 无法做 per-sample selection → 这是定义，不是发现。真正的实证发现只有：logprob 也失败了（因为 score compression）。论文用 12 页包装了一个 1 页就能说清的实证发现 + 4 页必然成立的推论。审稿人每轮都能感受到这种"不对称"，但因为每轮修改确实改善了某个表面问题，所以没法确切说哪里不对——只觉得"不够"。

(B) **没有 "so what" 时刻。** 论文诊断了 score compression 是瓶颈，然后……停了。非 tied 子集 +2.9pp 是全文最有力的证据，但它被埋在 Discussion 的一段话里，当作诊断工具而不是贡献。审稿人读完全文的感受是："OK，你告诉我这些信号不行，compression 是原因。然后呢？"Conclusion 列了 4 个 future direction（verifiers, relaxed decoding, 70B, conformal），等于承认论文本身没有前进一步。

(C) **Systematic comparison 不是贡献。** 5 信号 × 3 数据集 × 2 模型的全景表格是方法论基础设施，不是学术贡献。Difficulty-dependent signal ranking 是有用的实践洞见，但在竞争激烈的 venue 里不够 novel。

**简言之：论文花 12 页说了"这条路不通"，但没说"哪条路通"。6 轮 framing 优化解决不了这个问题，因为问题不在 frame，在 content。**

## 2. 什么会让审稿人给 4/5

**审稿人从 3→4 的心理转变是："这篇论文教了我一个我不知道的事，而且这个事 matters。"**

当前论文的问题：
- "信号不能选" → 80% 是定义性的 → "你在告诉我水往低处流"
- "Score compression 是原因" → 有趣但不完整 → "原因找到了，然后呢？"
- "Non-tied subset +2.9pp" → 最有价值但被埋 → "你已经找到了解药的线索，为什么不追下去？"

**让审稿人给 4/5 的关键缺失：验证 score compression 确实是唯一/主要瓶颈的 controlled ablation。**

具体来说：如果论文能展示"移除 constrained decoding 后 logprob selection 恢复效力"，则：
- Gap 从"observation"升级为"mechanism with controlled evidence"
- "Under constrained decoding"的 scope 从被动限制变为主动发现
- 给出了明确的 mitigation path（relaxed decoding + post-hoc filtering）
- Non-tied subset 从 diagnostic crumb 变为 mechanism confirmation 的一部分

## 3. 大实验评估

**(a) Free-form decoding 对照实验 — 强烈推荐，ROI 最高**

这是能打破 3.0 天花板的单一实验。两种结果都让论文更强：
- 如果 free-form 下 gap 消失/缩小 → 论文变成"constrained decoding creates a selection bottleneck"——一个关于 decoding regime 的发现，比"signals don't work for IE"更 general、更 impactful
- 如果 free-form 下 gap 仍在 → 论文变成"selection is fundamentally hard for structured IE"——scope 从 regime-specific 升级为 universal finding

**实现方案：**
- 在 SciERC 上重跑 Qwen3-8B sampling，去掉 Outlines constrained decoding
- Fine-tuned 模型在 free-form 下大概率 80-95% outputs 可解析（JSON 格式在训练数据里学过）
- 对 parseable outputs 计算 logprob variance、selection performance、QE metrics
- 对比 constrained vs free-form 的 logprob 分布

**成本：** SciERC 529 instances × 8 samples ≈ 4232 次生成。8B 模型在 5090 上大约 1-2 小时。分析 CPU 分钟级。**总计 < 4 小时。**

**(b) 70B 模型 — 中等推荐**

回答"更大模型是否有不同行为"。但成本高（需要多卡、更长推理时间），且如果结论不变则 marginal gain；如果结论变了则需要重构全文。**在 (a) 之后考虑。**

**(c) 更多 RE 数据集 — 低优先**

解决单数据集弱点，但不改变核心贡献。"preliminary" 标注已足够诚实。**DDL 前不建议。**

**(d) Supervised verifier baseline — 高推荐但成本更大**

训一个小 verifier（DeBERTa or 8B classification head）在现有 (input, output, F1) 数据上。如果 verifier 能 partially close the gap：
- 证明 gap IS closable → negative finding 变 actionable
- 给出 upper bound → 读者知道"unsupervised 方法还差多远"

**成本：** 实现 + 训练 + 评估约 1-2 天。**如果 (a) 做完后还有时间，做这个。**

**(e) Temperature/sampling 消融 — 低推荐**

已有 T=0.7 vs T=1.0 数据，差异不大。更宽的 sweep 不太可能改变结论。**(a) 已更直接地测试 compression mechanism。**

**(f) 补充方案：hybrid decoding**

如果 (a) 确认 free-form 下 logprob selection 有效，自然的下一步是：
- Free-form 生成 → 用 logprob 选 → 对选中的 output 做 post-hoc JSON 解析/修正
- 或：constrained + free-form 并行生成，用 free-form logprob 排序 constrained outputs

这提供了一个 **practical solution**，将论文从纯 negative 转为 constructive。**取决于 (a) 的结果。**

## 4. 优先级排序

| 优先级 | 实验 | 预计耗时 | 预期 impact |
|--------|------|----------|------------|
| **P0** | (a) Free-form decoding ablation | 2-4h GPU + 1h 分析 | **突破性** — 唯一能从 3.0→4.0 的实验 |
| P1 | (d) Simple verifier baseline | 1-2 天 | 高 — 添加 solution path |
| P2 | (b) 70B 模型 | 4-8h GPU | 中 — 如果 (a) 做完有余量 |
| Skip | (c)(e) | — | 低 — DDL 前不值得 |
| 条件 | (f) Hybrid decoding | 2-4h | 取决于 (a) 结果 |

## 5. 论文定位反思

**当前定位是评分天花板的主要原因。** "Systematic comparison + negative finding + mechanistic diagnosis" 在 Findings 的天花板大约在 3.5。

**推荐重定位**（如果 (a) 实验支持）：

"Identifying, diagnosing, and experimentally verifying a regime-specific selection bottleneck in constrained-decoding IE"

- C1: Gap 发现 + compression mechanism + **free-form ablation 验证**（不再是"我们发现了一个问题"，而是"我们通过 controlled ablation 证明了 constrained decoding 是 bottleneck"）
- C2: QE framework（降级为方法论贡献，但保留 difficulty-dependent findings）
- C3: Practical implications（从"future work"到"mitigation path"：在非 tied 实例上用 logprob；考虑 relaxed decoding 或 verifier）

**标题可能需要调整**（取决于 (a) 结果），如：
"The Constrained Decoding Bottleneck: Why Confidence Signals Predict but Cannot Select in Information Extraction"

## 6. 总结

6 轮 3.0/5 的根因是 **content ceiling，不是 framing ceiling**。继续打磨同一组发现的呈现方式是 diminishing returns。Free-form decoding ablation 是成本最低（< 4 小时）、潜在 impact 最大的突破口。强烈建议在继续 D070 writing 修订的同时，立即启动实验 (a)。如果 (a) 结果支持 regime-specific bottleneck 假设，全文重构可以在结果到手后 24h 内完成。

content.thinking:
The Worker found that Qwen3 thinking tokens were indeed activated during SciERC training. Key findings:

1. `enable_thinking` was NOT set in SciERC training configs (ft_001/ft_002/ft_002_v2)
2. LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 defaults to `True`
3. Empty `<think>\n</think>\n\n` (~4-5 tokens) was injected before each response
4. These tokens were included in loss computation
5. CoNLL/WNUT had `enable_thinking=false` (thinking tokens in prompt side, no loss)


6. At inference, `enable_thinking=False` with XGrammar constrained decoding successfully prevents thinking tokens from appearing, and while there's a minor train-test mismatch from the empty thinking blocks during training, the practical impact is negligible since those blocks contained nothing.

This confirms the concern raised in Limitations—thinking tokens were activated for SciERC but not for CoNLL/WNUT, creating an inconsistency between the two training setups. However, the real-world effect is minimal given the empty thinking blocks and inference-time constraints. For the paper, I need to acknowledge this as a confound that should be documented.

The current Limitations section says thinking tokens "were not explicitly disabled," but now I have confirmation they were actually active during SciERC training. I should update this to reflect that thinking tokens were present (always-empty blocks injected before responses) rather than just not disabled. Since the D070 plan suggested moving this detail from a footnote into §4.1 Setup, that makes sense now that I have concrete evidence. Let me check whether the other two workers have finished their results.

import json
import os
import re
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "code"))

def parse_args():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Free-form decoding ablation for structured IE")
    p.add_argument("--model_path", type=str,
                    default="checkpoints/qwen3-8b-scierc-merged-v2")
    p.add_argument("--data_dir", type=str, default="data/scierc/processed_data")
    p.add_argument("--output_dir", type=str, default="results/exp_freeform_ablation")
    p.add_argument("--num_samples", type=int, default=8)

    p.add_argument("--num_test", type=int, default=99999)
    return p.parse_args()


def try_parse_json(raw_text):
    """Attempt JSON extraction from free-form text. Returns (dict_or_None, success)."""
    text = raw_text.strip()

    # Direct parse
    try:
        data = json.loads(text)
        if isinstance(data, dict):
            return data, True
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        pass

    # Find outermost { ... }
    start = text.find("{")
    end = text.rfind("}")
    if start != -1 and end > start:
        try:
            data = json.loads(text[start:end + 1])
            if isinstance(data, dict):
                return data, True
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            pass

    # Regex for ```json ... ``` blocks
    m = re.search(r'```(?:json)?\s*(\{.*?\})\s*```', text, re.DOTALL)
    if m:
        try:
            data = json.loads(m.group(1))
            if isinstance(data, dict):
                return data, True
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            pass

4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).

8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
9	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
10	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
11	\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
Under constrained decoding, LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
The LP compression mechanism is a direct consequence of constrained decoding's restricted token space; alternative decoding strategies may yield different LP distributions.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Toward mechanistic confirmation.}
Our diagnosis predicts that LP score compression should diminish under free-form (unconstrained) generation, where the full token vocabulary is available at each step.
A controlled ablation---comparing LP selection under constrained versus free-form decoding on identical instances, with post-hoc JSON parsing for the free-form condition---would directly test whether the bottleneck is decoding-regime-specific.
\textit{[Planned experiment: free-form ablation on SciERC NER/RE.]}
All findings reported in this paper are specific to the constrained decoding regime; whether the gap persists under relaxed or free-form decoding remains an open question.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses LP resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction, but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we evaluate five confidence signals from three families across NER and relation extraction on three benchmarks with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation, yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank candidates; the key empirical question is whether log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---or consensus-proximity selection can bridge this gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties for 60\% of instances under constrained decoding, while consensus-proximity (MBR decoding) fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Where log-probability compression is absent, selection recovers significant gains ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), identifying constrained-decoding score compression as the primary bottleneck.
Signal rankings further depend on task complexity, with findings consistent across model families.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
5	More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
6	These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
7	For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
8	But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
9	The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
10	There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
11	Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?
12	
13	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
14	These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
15	Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
16	The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
17	Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.
18	
19	Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs are unparseable.
20	All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.
21	
22	Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): under constrained decoding, consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
23	By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input, precluding per-sample discrimination.
24	The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection---instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding} with structural utility functions---can recover discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
25	Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability is severely compressed under constrained decoding (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
26	Our findings are specific to the constrained decoding regime; whether the gap persists under free-form generation remains an open question.
27	
28	\begin{figure*}[t]
29	\centering
30	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
31	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1. \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, precluding sample selection. Consensus-proximity selection does not recover per-sample discrimination.}
32	\label{fig:overview}
33	\end{figure*}
34	
35	We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
36	Our contributions are:
37	\begin{enumerate}
38	    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap and its diagnosis.}
39	    We demonstrate that strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$, AUROC${=}0.75$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom) under constrained decoding.
40	    Log-probability---the only per-sample signal---fails due to score compression (60\% of instances effectively tied); where compression is mitigated, it becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
41	    Consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) also fails to bridge the gap.
42	
43	    \item \textbf{A systematic evaluation framework.}
44	    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection, showing that these metrics decouple and single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
45	
46	    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
47	    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
48	    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$), indicating overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs are unparseable.
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): under constrained decoding, consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input, precluding per-sample discrimination.
The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection---instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding} with structural utility functions---can recover discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability is severely compressed under constrained decoding (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
Our findings are specific to the constrained decoding regime; whether the gap persists under free-form generation remains an open question.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1. \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, precluding sample selection. Consensus-proximity selection does not recover per-sample discrimination.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap and its diagnosis.}
    We demonstrate that strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$, AUROC${=}0.75$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom) under constrained decoding.
    Log-probability---the only per-sample signal---fails due to score compression (60\% of instances effectively tied); where compression is mitigated, it becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
    Consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) also fails to bridge the gap.

    \item \textbf{A systematic evaluation framework.}
    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection, showing that these metrics decouple and single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$), indicating overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Within the constrained decoding regime standard for structured IE, we demonstrate that consistency signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input; log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails ($p{>}0.39$) despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom due to constrained-decoding-induced score compression.
Where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$); consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) similarly fails as utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty, with consistent ordering across two model families at 8B scale.
RE findings rest on SciERC alone (preliminary, single benchmark) and warrant multi-benchmark validation.
A direct free-form generation ablation would confirm whether the bottleneck is decoding-regime-specific.
Trained verifiers, relaxed decoding constraints, scaling to 70B+ models, and conformal prediction are promising directions for closing the gap.
